title: For Every Complex Problem There Is an Answer That Is Clear, Simple, and Wrong
author: Regenerative Schools
summary: Writing three weeks into a new principal role in a new country, the author reflects on the tension between confident action and humble inquiry that faces any leader entering an unfamiliar school. Drawing on 15 years of leadership across four countries, she argues that overconfident leaders who diagnose and fix problems too quickly typically misdiagnose them and create chaos, while a root cause of this overconfidence is treating schools as 'complicated' predictable machines rather than 'complex' ecosystems where identical interventions produce different results in different contexts. She cites Isa Rose Florez's claim that schools' core problem is a 'tenacious fixation on complicated, reductionist, machine-based thinking' and H.L. Mencken's line that clear, simple answers to complex problems are usually wrong, using both to explain why copied solutions, whether an imported pet program or a scripted curriculum, consistently underperform. In response, she describes a concrete transition plan modeled on Michael Watkins's The First 90 Days: repeated classroom walkthroughs, one-on-one meetings with every staff member in her section, time with students at recess and lunch, and parent 'tea with the principal' sessions, all built around three deliberately humble questions she is training herself to ask instead of asserting solutions.
points: The essay's central distinction, between 'complicated' systems (predictable, machine-like, where fixes transfer across contexts) and 'complex' systems (ecosystem-like, where identical interventions produce unpredictable, context-dependent results), reframes why copied 'best practice' programs so often fail in new schools.

The author names a specific and common leadership failure mode: senior leaders entering a new school confident they already know what's broken, who misdiagnose problems and generate chaos and teacher burnout rather than solutions.

She operationalizes 'humble inquiry' into a concrete 90-day entry plan (repeated classroom walkthroughs, individual staff meetings, recess and lunch time with students, parent 'tea with the principal' sessions) rather than leaving it as an abstract leadership virtue.

Three specific phrases ('Help me understand the thinking behind this,' 'Tell me more,' 'What might I be missing?') are offered as trainable habits of inquiry a leader can practice deliberately rather than a personality trait.
The piece explicitly frames this as a polarity to be balanced, not resolved, acknowledging that too much inquiry produces its own failure mode of overthinking and inaction.
quotes: I've watched as senior leaders come into a new school so sure that they know what's broken and how to fix it, only to misdiagnose problems and create chaos instead of solutions, adding to teacher burnout.

Complexity is the purview of living beings, and is not nearly so neat or predictable. In an ecosystem, community, or classroom, each part is connected in too many messy and hidden ways to be able to reliably predict outcomes.

Isa Rose Florez, in her recent book The End of Education as We Know It, goes so far as to assert that 'the root problem with schools today is their tenacious fixation on complicated, reductionist, machine-based thinking.'

In fact, I've never seen a solution copied exactly from one context to another that works as intended: whether leaders who come into a new school fixated on a particular program they want to implement, or teachers who are handed a scripted curriculum that they're supposed to deliver word-for-word.
Like H.L. Mencken said, 'For every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple and wrong.'

Effective leaders strike the right balance between doing (making things happen) and being (observing and reflecting). Planning to learn means figuring out in advance what the important questions are and how you can best answer them.
